new_statements.quote: b) Un point sur une voyelle ou à la droite d'une voyelle marque la pla[ce] de l'accent dynamique. Comme celui-ci est presque toujours sur la pre[mière] syllabe, il ne sera marqué que dans les cas qui font exception à cette [règle]. — 4. Accents toniques. Dans le Kukuruku, il y a trois accents toniques: L'accent tonique haut, désigné par ´. L'accent tonique bas, désigné par `. L'accent tonique montant, désigné par ˇ. Une voyelle sans signe est brève et a l'accent tonique moyen [...] (p. 452). — [...] le radical du verbe reçoit un accent tonique bas; l'accent dynamique se pose généralement sur la première syllabe. (p. 889, §37)
new_statements.translation: b) A dot on a vowel or to the right of a vowel marks the place of the dynamic accent [= stress]. Since this is almost always on the first syllable, it will be marked only in the cases which are exceptions to this rule. — 4. Tonal accents. In Kukuruku there are three tonal accents: the high tonal accent, marked ´; the low tonal accent, marked `; the rising tonal accent, marked ˇ. A vowel without a sign is short and has the mid tonal accent [...] (p. 452). — [...] the verb root receives a low tonal accent; the dynamic accent is generally placed on the first syllable. (p. 889, §37). Bracketed letters restore line-ends clipped in the scan's right margin.
new_statements.citation: Strub, P. Eugène. 1915/1916. Essai d'une grammaire de la langue Kukuruku (Nigeria, Afrique Occidentale). Anthropos 10/11: 450-465, 888-907.
new_statements.locator: Anthropos 10 (1915), p. 452, Première partie, Chapitre I 'Les sons', §3 'Quantité des syllabes. — Accent dynamique', (b), and §4 'Accents toniques'; corroborated p. 889 (Anthropos 11, 1916), §37; PDF pages 3 and 18 of the saved scan
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (36-page Rosetta Project scan of Anthropos 10/11, open item rosettaproject_ets_morsyn-2) and rendered PDF pages 1, 2, 3, 17, 18 to images (printed pp. 450, 451, 452, 888, 889) and read them directly, alongside the held scanned file. The quoted passage is on p. 452 (PDF page 3) exactly as stated: heading '3. Quantité des syllabes. — Accent dynamique.', item 'b) Un point sur une voyelle ou à la droite d'une voyelle marque la place de l'accent dynamique. Comme celui-ci est presque toujours sur la première syllabe, il ne sera marqué que dans les cas qui font exception à cette règle.' followed by '4. Accents toniques. Dans le Kukuruku, il y a trois accents toniques: L'accent tonique haut,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The language is tonal (Strub: three marked tones high, low, rising, plus unmarked mid; modern sources: two underlying tones, five surface pitches). Separately from tone, Strub reports a 'dynamic accent' (stress) that falls almost always on the first syllable of the word, marked in his notation only when it falls elsewhere.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as such. Ch. VIII §34A (p. 888) states that within one word there can never be two dynamic accents on two consecutive syllables, and in two-word combinations either word may keep or lose its stress under vowel elision; §34B lists the four possible stress placements in pairs of bisyllabic words (first or second syllable of each).
new_statements.exceptions: Words with stress off the first syllable exist and are marked with a dot (p. 452); elision and euphony suppress 'a certain number of encumbering dynamic accents' and modify tones in connected speech (p. 888, §34); in combinations b-d of bisyllabic words the stress may sit on the second syllable of a word (p. 888); §37 says 'généralement' (generally) rather than 'always' for deverbal nouns (p. 889).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement ('accent dynamique' = stress vs 'accent tonique' = tone), with phrase-level adjustments described for two-word combinations (Ch. VIII). Missionary description (Société des Missions Africaines de Lyon) of 'Kukuruku' = the Wano dialect of Agenigbodi/Agenebode (Weppa-Wano clan) per Thomas 1910: 143. The modern descriptions (Laver 1967, Elimelech 1976/1978) are silent on stress and treat the language as purely tonal, so Strub's stress claim is unconfirmed by later work.
new_statements.identity_note: Strub's 'Kukuruku' is, per Thomas 1910: 143 ('the Wano language (Agenigbodi) derived from Father Strub'), the Weppa-Wano dialect of Etsako spoken at Agenebode — a dialect of Yekhee (yekh1238), not a separate language. Laver 1967 describes the Aviele (Ayele) dialect near Agbede; Elimelech 1976/1978 focuses on Ekpheli with data from eight dialects. All fall under yekh1238; Glottolog gives no separate dialect codes that I saw.

sources.note: Ch. I §3 'Quantité des syllabes. — Accent dynamique' (p. 452): the dynamic accent (stress) is almost always on the first syllable and is written (a dot) only where it is not; §4 (p. 452): three tonal accents high/low/rising plus unmarked mid, i.e. a tone language with a separate stress statement; Ch. VIII §34-36 (pp. 888-889) give rules for stress in two-word combinations (no two stresses on consecutive syllables within a word; either word may lose its stress under elision); §37 (p. 889) 'l'accent dynamique se pose généralement sur la première syllabe'.

sources.note: Silent. scanned of Ch. I Introduction and Ch. II Segmental Phonology (pp. 1-15, incl. 2.0 'Phonetic correlates'), Ch. III The Tonal System (pp. 41-54) and the bibliography (pp. 165-170) contains no occurrence of 'stress', 'accent', 'intensity', 'loudness' or 'prominence'. Describes Ekpheli dialect: five surface tones (H, L, falling, rising, downstep), two underlying tones, downdrift/downstep; reviews Laver 1967/1969 and Elugbe 1973 as the only earlier phonologies.

sources.citation: Laver, John. 1967. A preliminary phonology of the Ayele dialect of Esako. Journal of West African Languages 4(2): 53-56.
sources.note: Silent on stress. Sections: consonant phonemes (tense/lax/neutral with consonant harmony), vowel phonemes, Tones ('ayele Esako has four tones in this analysis: high, low, high fall, and downstep'; downdrift within the breath-group), syllable structure (V, CV, CCV), word list. No mention of stress or accent. Aviele (Ayele) dialect, Agbede area.

sources.citation: Thomas, Northcote W. 1910. Anthropological Report on the Edo-speaking Peoples of Nigeria, Part II: Linguistics. London: Harrison and Sons.
sources.note: The 'Accent and tone' paragraph (pp. 141-142: 'The dynamic accent falls normally on the penultimate, but in words ending in ia, ie, oa, ua, etc., it usually falls on the antepenultimate') sits in the EDO (Bini) grammar section and is not about Kukuruku/Etsako. Appendix A 'Wano Grammar' (pp. 143-146, 'derived from Father Strub', i.e. the Etsako dialect of Agenigbodi/Agenebode) gives consonants, vowels, plurals and adjectives only — no accent statement. Kukuruku texts pp. 78-113 have no phonology.
